extracted.intended_audience: Employers, workers, attorneys, compliance officers, and regulators affected by U.S. non‑compete clauses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and substantive legal standards in the FTC's Final Rule (16 CFR Part 910) that define non‑compete clauses, identify covered persons and workers (including senior executive carveouts), enumerate prohibited conduct, list exceptions and notice requirements, and describe preemption, enforcement, and regulatory analyses for compliance. Relevant to drafting, enforcing, rescinding, or responding to non‑compete clauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “Non‑Compete Clause”
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule defines “non‑compete clause” as “a term or condition of employment that prohibits a worker from, penalizes a worker for, or functions to prevent a worker from (1) seeking or accepting work in the United States with a different person where such work would begin after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition; or (2) operating a business in the United States after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For purposes of the final rule, “term or condition of employment” includes, but is not limited to, a contractual term or workplace policy, whether written or oral. The scope is functional (any term that operates to prevent future work/operation in the U.S.), not limited to labeled agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “Worker”
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule defines “worker” as “a natural person who works or who previously worked, whether paid or unpaid, without regard to the worker's title or the worker's status under any other State or Federal laws, including, but not limited to, whether the worker is an employee, independent contractor, extern, intern, volunteer, apprentice, or a sole proprietor who provides a service to a person.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition explicitly includes a natural person who works for a franchisee or franchisor, but does not include a franchisee in the context of a franchisee‑franchisor relationship. The rule focuses on the person's work relationship, not labels used by employers or other statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of “Senior Executive” (two‑part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule adopts a two‑part test to define “senior executive” (job duties + compensation threshold) and explains the need for a two‑part test and how the final rule defines senior executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule permits existing non‑competes with senior executives to remain in force, and treats post‑effective‑date non‑competes for senior executives differently from other workers. See separate metrics for compensation threshold and job‑duties component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior Executive: Compensation Threshold (definition of “total annual compensation” and “preceding year”)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule defines the compensation threshold component of the senior executive test (definitions of “total annual compensation” and “preceding year”) used to determine whether a worker is a senior executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule discusses alternative compensation thresholds proposed and explains which periods/counting methods are used to determine whether a worker meets the threshold; agencies and employers should apply the specified definitions when assessing senior executive status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior Executive: Job Duties Component (officer, policy‑making authority, policy‑making position)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule defines the job duties component for senior executives, including definitions/explanations for terms like “officer,” “policy‑making authority,” and “policy‑making position.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission reviews alternative proposed job duties tests and explains how duties are evaluated; this component must be applied alongside the compensation threshold to determine senior executive status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions for Workers Other Than Senior Executives (§ 910.2(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: For a worker other than a senior executive, the final rule provides it is an unfair method of competition for a person to enter into or attempt to enter into a non‑compete clause; to enforce or attempt to enforce a non‑compete clause; or to represent that the worker is subject to a non‑compete clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission finds non‑competes with non‑senior workers to be restrictive, exploitative/coercive, and tending to negatively affect competitive conditions. The rule applies to non‑competes entered on or after the effective date (ban on new agreements) and renders existing non‑competes for these workers unenforceable after the effective date, subject to notice requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions for Senior Executives (§ 910.2(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: With respect to a senior executive, it is an unfair method of competition for a person to enter into or attempt to enter into a non‑compete clause; to enforce or attempt to enforce a non‑compete clause entered into after the effective date; or to represent that the senior executive is subject to a non‑compete clause where the non‑compete was entered into after the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing non‑competes entered before the effective date can remain in force for senior executives. The Commission explains why senior executives are treated differently (less likely to suffer acute ongoing harms and practical impacts of extinguishing agreements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Existing Non‑Competes (senior executives vs. other workers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Existing non‑competes entered before the effective date remain enforceable for senior executives but are not enforceable after the effective date for workers who are not senior executives. Employers must provide notice to workers for whom existing non‑competes are no longer enforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To facilitate compliance and minimize burden, the final rule includes model language that satisfies the notice requirement (Figure 1 to Paragraph (b)(4)). The final rule does not require rescission (legal modification) of existing non‑competes for senior executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice Requirement for Existing Non‑Competes (§ 910.2(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule includes a notice requirement for existing non‑competes (for non‑senior executives made unenforceable) — employers must notify affected workers that their existing non‑competes are no longer enforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule includes model language that satisfies the notice requirement to reduce compliance burden and administrative costs. The regulatory analysis estimates legal and administrative costs associated with notification and discusses methods for delivering notices (including mailed notice assumptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good‑Faith Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule provides it is not an unfair method of competition to enforce or attempt to enforce a non‑compete or to make representations about a non‑compete where a person has a good‑faith basis to believe that the final rule is inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits enforcement/actions in circumstances where a reasonable, good‑faith interpretation is that the rule does not apply (e.g., bona fide sale exception, causes of action accrued pre‑effective date, or other legitimate grounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of Business Exception (§ 910.3(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 910.3(a) provides an exception for non‑competes entered into by a person pursuant to a bona fide sale of a business entity (these are not covered by the final rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission discusses proposed language, comments received, and the final rule’s parameters for what constitutes a bona fide sale, to ensure that legitimate transactions transferring businesses are not swept up by the ban.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for Existing Causes of Action (§ 910.3(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not apply where a cause of action related to a non‑compete accrued prior to the effective date (existing causes of action exception, covering retroactivity, takings, due process concerns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission explains retroactivity limits and addresses comments on takings and due process; enforcement of pre‑existing causes of action is preserved subject to legal limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good Faith Exception/Requests To Expand or Narrow Coverage (§ 910.3 and V.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule includes and evaluates requests to expand coverage or to provide exceptions (e.g., differentiation by worker compensation/skills, access to information, industry exceptions such as healthcare, franchisor/franchisee relationships, covered market participants with competitors outside FTC jurisdiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission analyzes comments and explains why certain exceptions were accepted or rejected. Employers/industries seeking carveouts should review the Commission’s responses and evidence requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to State Laws and Preemption (§ 910.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not limit or affect enforcement of State laws that restrict non‑competes where the State laws do not conflict with the final rule, but it preempts State laws that conflict with the final rule. The rule discusses authority for preemption, benefits of preemption, and the extent of preemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entities must assess whether state law conflicts with the federal rule; where state law is more protective and does not conflict, it remains in effect. The Commission explains preemption boundaries and preservation of some state authority and private rights of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severability Clause (§ 910.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule includes a severability clause clarifying the Commission's intent that, if a reviewing court holds any part of the rule invalid or unenforceable, the remainder of the final rule shall remain in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The clause covers aspects such as particular restrictions, definitions, or standards for categories of workers; agencies and regulated parties should plan compliance assuming most of the rule survives challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Date and Compliance Timeline (Effective Date: Sept 4, 2024)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule is effective September 4, 2024. The document explains proposed vs. final effective dates and summarizes comments and the Commission’s decisions regarding timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers should implement compliance measures, notification processes, and operational changes in time to satisfy the effective date; regulatory analyses estimate costs and timelines associated with compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical Framework & Findings: Non‑Competes as Unfair Methods of Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission sets out an analytical framework and empirical findings that non‑competes are a method of competition (not a market condition), are facially unfair (restrictive/exclusionary; exploitative/coercive), and tend to negatively affect competitive conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule summarizes evidence and responses to comments; these findings are the factual/legal basis for treating specified practices as unfair under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms Identified: Suppression of Labor Mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds that non‑competes tend to suppress labor mobility (evidence and comment responses are discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppressed labor mobility is treated as a competitive harm in labor markets and as a justification for the rule’s prohibitions on non‑competes with most workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms Identified: Suppression of Workers' Earnings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds that non‑competes suppress workers’ earnings (empirical evidence, comment responses summarized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earnings suppression is a central component of the Commission’s economic rationale for the rule and is used in benefit–cost and distributional analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms Identified: Reduction in Job Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds that non‑competes reduce job quality for workers subject to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduced job quality is analyzed alongside mobility and earnings harms when assessing the rule’s projected benefits to workers and the economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms Identified: Inhibition of New Business Formation and Innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission finds that non‑competes inhibit new business formation and innovation (discusses evidence, comments, and Commission responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule’s expected pro‑competitive benefits include increased entrepreneurship and innovation; analyses estimate effects on firm entry and innovation metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms Identified: Potential Increases in Market Concentration and Consumer Prices; Reduced Quality/Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule identifies that non‑competes may increase market concentration and consumer prices and may reduce product/service quality and consumer choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These potential product/service‑market harms are part of the justification that non‑competes harm competition beyond labor markets; they inform the regulatory impact analysis and alternative evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives to Non‑Competes (trade secrets, NDAs, other protections)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission discusses that employers have alternatives to non‑competes to protect investments, including trade secret law, nondisclosure agreements (NDAs), and other means of protecting human and physical capital investments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission evaluates these alternatives (including empirical evidence and comments) and concludes that asserted justifications for non‑competes do not outweigh the harms; employers should consider these alternatives when revising policies post‑effective date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Analysis: Estimating Affected Workforce, Benefits, Costs, Distributional Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule contains a detailed regulatory analysis including methods for estimating the affected workforce, effects on enforceability metrics, benefits (earnings, innovation, prices), costs (human capital investment, legal/administrative costs, litigation effects), transfers, distributional effects, and break‑even analyses under alternative assumptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulated entities and commentators should consult the regulatory analysis sections for the Commission’s quantitative assumptions, illustrative examples (e.g., 'ten workers' notice cost example), and sensitivity analyses used to support the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction and Notification Administrative Requirements (PRA & RFA considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule discusses Paperwork Reduction Act compliance, projected reporting/recordkeeping/administrative costs for notification requirements, legal costs, and the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analysis regarding effects on small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers — particularly small businesses — should review PRA and RFA sections to understand expected administrative burdens and any illustrative cost estimates; the Commission includes discussion of significant alternatives and comment responses relating to small entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model Notice Language (Figure 1 to Paragraph (b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule includes model language (Figure 1 to Paragraph (b)(4)) intended to satisfy the notice requirement to workers whose existing non‑competes are no longer enforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using the model language satisfies the notice requirement and minimizes legal/administrative uncertainty; employers may rely on the provided model to reduce compliance risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope/Geographic Application and International Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule addresses coverage of work and business operations 'in the United States,' and discusses international application of the rule and related comments and Commission responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule clarifies territorial limits (focus on U.S. work/operations) and addresses cross‑border concerns and choice‑of‑law complications; entities with international operations should consult the rule’s discussion of international application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement Basis: Section 5 Unfair Methods of Competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule grounds prohibitions in Section 5 of the FTC Act, treating specified non‑compete practices as unfair methods of competition subject to FTC enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations may be addressed through FTC enforcement mechanisms; the rule also discusses interplay with private litigation, pre‑existing causes of action, and potential litigation effects analyzed in the regulatory analysis.
